Reviewer Response Analyses¶

Setup¶

n_samples=6768, n_features=84, n_proteins=376, n_npunid=18, enriched_rate=0.391

Shared helpers¶

Confidence intervals across folds, out-of-fold prediction for an arbitrary model, and the metric set used throughout. Every section below reuses these, so all reported numbers are produced by the same code path.

Major 1. Leave-one-nanoparticle-out validation¶

The analysis includes many protein-nanoparticle observations, but only 11 unique nanoparticles. Therefore, conclusions about zeta potential, size, core material, and surface coating are based on a very small nanoparticle sample. The authors should emphasize this limitation and provide leave-one-nanoparticle-out validation or nanoparticle-level resampling.

npunid is not a nanoparticle, it is a nanoparticle x incubation-concentration condition.

npunid 23 and 30 are the same nanoparticle, run at 40 and 4 mg/mL, but the excel file records d_TEM as 182 nm for one and 244 nm for the other. The two are merged here for grouping only: the dtem column is left exactly as recorded, so no model input changes and the merge affects fold membership alone.

Performance survives strict leave-one-nanoparticle-out. Going from 18 npunid folds to 11 material folds costs about 0.01 in both metrics (parsimonious model: R2 0.828 to 0.819, AUC 0.881 to 0.874), so the sibling leak is small, and the headline numbers do not depend on it.

The two weakest folds are both PS (AUC 0.700 and 0.775) and they are the only PS particles in the dataset, so nothing in training resembles them. That is the small-nanoparticle-sample limitation.

Major 2. Cross-validation grouping, per model¶

The manuscript gives different descriptions of how samples were grouped during cross-validation. It is unclear whether the regression model was grouped by nanoparticle or protein in all analyses. The authors should clearly describe the grouping method used for each model and ensure that feature selection is performed only within the training data.

Every observation in this dataset is a protein x nanoparticle pair, so rows are dependent along two axes at once: the 376 proteins and the nanoparticles.

Scheme used by each analysis in unified.ipynb¶

Analysis Model Resampling unit Scheme Metric
Bootstrap feature importance regressor protein (entry) cluster bootstrap, N = 500 Gini importance
Bootstrap feature importance classifier protein (entry) cluster bootstrap, N = 500 Gini importance
RFECV feature selection regressor nanoparticle (npunid) GroupKFold, 5 folds neg. MAE (log1p)
RFECV feature selection classifier protein (entry) GroupKFold, 10 folds ROC AUC
Permutation importance (OOF) classifier protein (entry) GroupKFold, 10 folds ROC AUC
Out-of-fold performance classifier protein (entry) GroupKFold, 10 folds ROC AUC, accuracy, F1
Out-of-fold performance regressor nanoparticle (npunid) leave-one-out, 18 folds R2, MAE, RMSE
SHAP, PDP/ICE, correlation heatmaps, protein clustering both none single fit on all rows descriptive only

The rule: the classifier is grouped by protein, the regressor by nanoparticle. The last row matters for reading the figures: SHAP, PDP/ICE and the zeta-sweep clustering are descriptions of a fitted model, not performance estimates, and are not cross-validated.

Why the two models are grouped differently¶

They answer different questions. The classifier asks "given a new serum protein, will it be enriched on a nanoparticle?", so proteins are held out. The regressor asks "given a new nanoparticle, what corona abundances will it produce?", so nanoparticles are held out. Grouping either model the other way answers a question we are not making claims about, and in the classifier's case is optimistic: protein identity is strongly predictive of enrichment, so leaving proteins in both train and test leaks.

The section below quantifies that, and adds a doubly-blocked scheme that holds out proteins and nanoparticles simultaneously. The most conservative estimate available from this design.

The grouping choice moves the result more than any modelling decision in this notebook. The same parsimonious model scores R2 0.42 / AUC 0.67 with proteins held out, R2 0.82 / AUC 0.87 with nanoparticles held out, and R2 0.48 / AUC 0.64 with both held out at once.

The gap is not overfitting, it is which axis carries the signal. Most features in the dataset are protein-level constants (quantified in Major 5), so holding out a nanoparticle leaves the protein term intact and the model keeps nearly all of its accuracy, while holding out a protein removes it.

Feature selection inside the training data¶

In unified.ipynb the RFECV selection runs once on all rows, and the parsimonious sets it produces (PARSI_7, PARSI_6) are then scored on those same rows. The reported numbers for the parsimonious models are therefore optimistic by an unknown amount.

The check below re-runs the selection inside each training fold only: for every outer fold, RFECV is fitted on the training rows, a model is fitted on the features it selects, and that model is scored on the held-out rows it never saw. The features chosen per fold are also recorded, which doubles as a selection-stability report: how often each feature survives when the selection cannot see the test data.

Selection bias is not what inflates these numbers. With RFECV refitted inside each training fold, nested ROC AUC is 0.679 +/- 0.057, indistinguishable from the 0.677 (full) and 0.668 (parsimonious) obtained with the published sets, so the optimism from selecting on all rows is smaller than the fold-to-fold noise. All seven PARSI_7 features survive in 90 to 100 % of folds, so the published set is reproducible when the test fold is invisible.

Major 5. Serum abundance as predictor and as label¶

Serum protein abundance is used as a predictor, but it is also used to calculate the enrichment label. This may explain why serum abundance is an important feature. The authors should compare the full model with a simple model using serum abundance alone and report how much additional value nanoparticle features provide.

Two separate things are being asked, and they need separate answers.

(a) Is the classifier circular? The label is enriched = (abundance / abundance_controls > 1), and abundance_controls is a predictor. So the label is a function of one of the inputs. The first cell below measures how far that alone gets you, with no model at all.

(b) What do nanoparticle features add? An ablation over the paper's own three feature families, plus serum abundance on its own, scored under both grouping schemes from Major 2.

The circularity concern applies to the classifier only. The regression target is measured corona abundance, which is not constructed from abundance_controls, so there the relationship is correlation rather than construction.

serum=1, nanoparticle=12, experimental=3, protein=68, total=84
constant within every protein: 69/84, varying: ['centrifuged', 'core_iron_oxide', 'core_iron_oxide_au', 'core_ps', 'dh_functionalized', 'dtem', 'incubation_concentration_mg_per_ml', 'ligand_carboxylate', 'ligand_citrate', 'ligand_peg_five_k', 'ligand_peg_two_k', 'ligand_pei', 'ligand_pvp', 'np_incubation_concentration_mg_per_ml', 'zeta_potential']

(a) How much of the label is recoverable from serum abundance alone?¶

No model, no threshold: sort every observation by abundance_controls and score that ordering directly against the label. ROC AUC of a raw feature is the probability that a randomly chosen enriched row outranks a randomly chosen non-enriched one, so it measures separation without anything being fitted. Its no-skill value is 0.5 whatever the class balance, because it compares within classes and the prevalence cancels. Unlike average precision in Major 8, whose no-skill value is the prevalence. The cross-validated one-feature random forest is the serum only (1) row of the ablation below, and appears again with confidence intervals in Major 8.

AUC, ranking by serum abundance (high -> enriched): 0.5673  [0.532, 0.602]
AUC, ranking by serum abundance (low  -> enriched): 0.4327
  95% CI from 1000 protein-cluster bootstrap resamples (SE 0.0176)

Spearman(serum abundance, corona abundance):        0.5882

Var(log2 serum) = 10.483, Var(log2 corona, nonzero rows) = 11.504, n nonzero = 3171/6768

Ranking by serum abundance alone gives AUC 0.567 [0.532, 0.602]: better than chance, since the interval excludes 0.5, but only slightly.

No model is fitted in this cell. It measures the raw ranking only. The cross-validated one-feature forest appears in the sections below with: AUC 0.454 in the serum only (1) row of the ablation in (b), and 0.454 [0.416, 0.497] in the RF, serum only row of Major 8. That interval excludes 0.5, so once a model has to generalise to held-out proteins, serum abundance alone ranks them slightly worse than chance - the direction the label definition predicts, since a high serum value makes the ratio harder to clear. So the circularity concern does not survive either measurement: if the label were an artefact of its own denominator, a model given that denominator would recover it, and none does.

The corona term also carries more spread than the serum term (11.50 against 10.48 on the log2 scale). The label is constructed from serum abundance but is not determined by it: which proteins exceed the ratio is set by the measured corona.

Nanoparticle features contribute little alone and matter through interactions. On their own they are worthless under nanoparticle-grouped CV (R2 0.000, AUC 0.529), which is expected: every nanoparticle feature is constant within a particle, so holding one out leaves them nothing to vary over. Added on top of everything else they are worth +0.047 R2 and +0.041 AUC, the largest marginal contribution of any family except protein.

The partition also explains Major 2. Exactly 69 of the 84 features are constant within every protein. The 15 that vary are the 12 nanoparticle features and the 3 experimental ones. Almost all of the information is carried on the protein axis, which is why holding out a nanoparticle costs so much less than holding out a protein.

Serum abundance behaves in the opposite way. Alone it already reaches R2 0.747, yet dropping it from the full set costs essentially nothing (-0.002 R2) because the 68 protein features carry the same information. Serum abundance is sufficient but not necessary, nanoparticle features are necessary but not sufficient, and the full model beats serum alone by 0.067 R2 (0.747 to 0.813).

Major 7. Evidence for dropping PEI¶

Figures 2 and 7 appear to show correlations between feature-importance values rather than correlations between the actual experimental features. These results do not directly show physical or biological relationships. The authors should clarify this point and provide stronger evidence before removing features such as PEI.

Two independent lines of evidence follow:

  1. Measured relationship between the two variables
  2. Paired performance comparison of every model variant

Evidence 1. The two variables are not merely correlated, they are redundant by construction¶

ligand_pei is a binary coating indicator and zeta_potential is continuous, evaluated at the 18 nanoparticle conditions.

Spearman(zeta_potential, ligand_pei) = 0.8212  (p = 0.00e+00)

Zeta potential by PEI coating, across the 18 NP conditions:
            count  min  max       mean
ligand_pei                            
0              12  -63   -3 -30.333333
1               6   12   39  26.666667

Separation: every PEI particle has zeta >= +12 mV, every non-PEI particle zeta <= -3 mV.
Any threshold in (-3, +12) mV recovers `ligand_pei` exactly: AUC(zeta -> PEI) = 1.000.

The two variables are not merely correlated, they are interchangeable. Every PEI-coated particle has a positive zeta potential (+12 to +39 mV) and every uncoated particle a negative one (-63 to -3 mV), so a single threshold anywhere in the gap reproduces ligand_pei exactly (AUC 1.000).

Evidence 2. Paired performance comparison¶

Four variants of the parsimonious set, scored out-of-fold under both grouping schemes from Major 2, compared fold by fold against the full 7-feature set so the difference carries an interval rather than being a single-point comparison.

If zeta_potential and ligand_pei are redundant, dropping either alone should cost nothing while dropping both should hurt.

Major 8. Predictive performance in full¶

The manuscript focuses on feature importance, but the predictive performance of the models is not presented in enough detail. The authors should report cross-validated regression metrics and classification metrics, including AUROC, precision-recall performance, calibration, and confidence intervals. Simple baseline models should also be included.

Everything below is out-of-fold. Each model is evaluated under both grouping schemes from Major 2.

Metrics are computed the way unified.ipynb computes them: pool every held-out prediction, then score once. Confidence intervals are 95 % percentile intervals from 1000 bootstrap resamples of the unit the scheme blocked on - proteins when proteins were held out, nanoparticle materials when nanoparticles were - so the interval belongs to the same estimator as the point estimate.

Baselines included: majority class and stratified guessing for the classifier, the training mean for the regressor, penalised and unpenalised linear models for both, and the single-feature serum-abundance model from Major 5.

Protein-grouped, the parsimonious forest reaches AUC 0.668 [0.634, 0.698] and average precision 0.588 [0.533, 0.643] against a prevalence floor of 0.391, above every baseline (majority class 0.500, logistic regression 0.556) and far below the 0.874 the nanoparticle-grouped scheme reports for the same model.

Calibration: mean predicted probability 0.390 against an observed rate of 0.391, with a maximum bin deviation of 0.070 versus 0.156 for logistic regression, so the predicted probabilities can be read as probabilities.

Serum abundance alone is below chance protein-grouped, AUC 0.454 [0.416, 0.497], and the interval excludes 0.5. That is the expected direction rather than an anomaly: the label is (corona / serum > 1), so a high serum value makes the ratio harder to clear.

Regression: metrics, confidence intervals, and random forest vs linear regression¶

The comparison the response document asks for. Ridge and LinearRegression are fitted on standardised features. The nanoparticle core and ligand indicators are collinear by construction, so the unpenalised fit is rank-deficient and solved by least squares.

With nanoparticles held out, the gain over a linear model is non-linearity rather than regularisation. The parsimonious forest reaches R2 0.819 [0.751, 0.876] against 0.447 for linear regression on the same six features and 0.502 for both ridge and unpenalised least squares on all 84. Ridge and OLS agree to three decimals, so the penalty is doing nothing and the whole difference is the functional form.

With proteins held out, that gain disappears. The forest (0.424 [0.209, 0.565]), linear regression (0.426 [0.267, 0.507]), ridge (0.409) and a forest given serum abundance alone (0.406 [0.066, 0.619]) are indistinguishable. Predicting abundance for an unseen protein is essentially predicting its serum abundance, and no model here does better than that. This is the same structural fact as Major 2 and Major 5 seen from a third angle - the regression generalises across nanoparticles, not across proteins.

Major 9. Number of clusters, cluster stability, and labelling¶

The authors selected three K-means clusters without clearly explaining why three was chosen. The labels "always" and "never" are also too strong because the average probabilities are not 1.0 or 0. The authors should justify the number of clusters, evaluate cluster stability, and use less absolute labels.

response matrices: detection (376, 6), enrichment (376, 6)

Choosing k: elbow and silhouette¶

Inertia plus mean silhouette width, which unlike inertia has an interior optimum and so can actually select a k.

Inertia falls smoothly with no elbow (85, 57, 38, 31 for detection), and the silhouette maximum is at k = 2 for both targets (0.582 and 0.537, against 0.495 and 0.448 at k = 3). For enrichment even k = 4 scores higher than k = 3.

Stability: does the same partition reappear under resampling?¶

For each k, refit K-means on 100 random 80 % subsamples of the proteins and compare each result with the reference partition restricted to the same proteins (adjusted Rand index). A partition that only exists in one particular sample of proteins will score poorly here. Per-cluster Jaccard similarity is also reported for k = 3, which shows whether all three clusters are stable or only some of them.

The detection clustering at k = 3 is solid: ARI 0.971 +/- 0.038 under 80 % protein subsampling, with every cluster above 0.94 Jaccard.

The enrichment clustering at k = 3 is the least stable choice anywhere in the range tested (ARI 0.733 +/- 0.275, against 0.997 at k = 2 and 0.959 at k = 4). The weak cluster is the intermediate one, Jaccard 0.644, so roughly a third of its membership changes from one resample to the next. The low and high clusters hold at 0.837 and 0.833. That is at least coherent with what the group is: proteins that sit firmly in neither mode.
